segments.text: We do not know what the builders of Giza called their sphinx. More than a thousand years later, Egyptians worshipped it as a god, Horemakhet, "Horus in the Horizon." Between its paws stands a stone set up by King Thutmose the Fourth. It tells how, as a young prince, he rested in the shadow of the great god. In a dream, the god promised him the kingdom, and said that the sand of the desert had reached him.

segments.text: But the play never gives the words of the riddle. We find them in later writers, such as Athenaeus, and a handbook of myths called the Library. They ask: what has one voice, and becomes four-footed, two-footed, and three-footed? The answer is a human being. A baby crawls, an adult walks, and the old lean on a staff. In these texts, there is no morning, noon, or evening. And when the riddle was solved, the Library says, the Sphinx threw herself down.
